damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Burrow morning arrival, Arthur meets Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 4–21: Arthur arrives exhausted from nine raids, slumps in a chair with glasses off, gropes for the teapot, and is genuinely caught off-guard by Harry's presence ('Harry? Harry who?'). His excitement about the flying car ('Did it go all right?') is spontaneous and then immediately suppressed under Molly's glare. He is physically worn, emotionally unguarded, and slightly absent-minded in a believable, human way.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: Arthur enters upright and alert, delivers 'What a night! Nine raids! Nine!' as a punchy one-liner, then immediately pivots to asking Harry about parking meters with cheerful energy. The exhausted, slumped, glasses-off physicality is gone. His 'Did it go all right?' beat is retained but the surrounding texture of genuine tiredness and domestic disorientation is stripped away.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes Arthur as a man who genuinely wears his demanding, undervalued job on his body. His physical exhaustion grounds his warmth and eccentricity in real sacrifice. The film compresses this into a punchline entrance, losing the sympathetic texture that makes his Muggle enthusiasm feel earned rather than comic-relief padding.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Arthur's loophole speech omitted at the Burrow
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 13–17: When cornered by Molly about the enchanted car, Arthur mounts a careful, slightly absurd legal defence ('there's a loophole in the law, you'll find… As long as he wasn't intending to fly the car…'), before Molly devastates him by pointing out he wrote the loophole himself. This exchange shows Arthur as simultaneously principled (technically correct), self-aware (he knows he's been caught), and endearingly sneaky — a man who games his own rules to feed his obsession.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: The loophole exchange is entirely absent. Molly simply tells Arthur what the boys did ('Your sons flew that enchanted car of yours to Surrey'), Arthur reacts with poorly-suppressed delight ('Did you now! How'd it go?!'), catches Molly's eye, and pivots to 'That was very wrong, boys.' The legal self-justification and the revelation that he wrote the loophole for himself are gone.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The loophole scene is one of the richest characterisation beats Arthur gets in the entire book. It shows he is not merely a bumbling enthusiast but someone with genuine cunning who applies his professional knowledge to personal ends — and who is self-aware enough to feel guilty about it. Removing it flattens him to a one-note 'Muggles are fascinating!' figure and weakens the Molly–Arthur dynamic, which depends on Molly exposing his deliberate mischief, not just his accidental enthusiasm.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Dinner-table Muggle interrogation reduced to a single parking-meter question
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 23–24: Over Harry's stay at the Burrow, Arthur repeatedly seats Harry beside him at dinner to 'bombard him with questions about life with Muggles' — plugs, the postal service, the telephone — responding with 'Fascinating… Ingenious, really, how many ways Muggles have found of getting along without magic.' This is a sustained pattern of intellectual curiosity and genuine respect, not comedy.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: Arthur's Muggle curiosity is condensed to one question about a parking meter immediately after arriving home from a night of raids, before the scene moves on. The repeated dinner-table ritual and the 'Ingenious' line are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but cumulative: the book uses Arthur's Muggle interest to show genuine cross-cultural respect and intellectual engagement. The film uses it as a quick comic beat. The distinction matters for understanding why his Muggle Protection Act is a moral commitment, not a quirk.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Arthur's glasses repair of Harry omitted at Diagon Alley reunion
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 54–55: When the family reunites with Harry outside Gringotts after his Floo mishap, 'Mr. Weasley took Harry's glasses, gave them a tap of his wand, and returned them, good as new.' A small but deliberate act of practical fatherly care directed specifically at Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1 (Diagon Alley): It is Hermione who repairs Harry's glasses with 'Oculus Reparo' when she meets him outside Gringotts. Arthur is present ('So you're dentists! Fascinating!') but performs no equivalent gesture toward Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the glasses repair as a quiet signal that Arthur instinctively acts as a surrogate father to Harry — noticing a practical need and fixing it without fuss. Transferring this action to Hermione (who turns it into a wand-skill demonstration) erases a small but meaningful data point in the Arthur–Harry surrogate-father relationship the books build across multiple volumes.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Flourish and Blotts brawl: Arthur restrained by Hagrid before throwing a punch
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 73: 'There was a thud of metal as Ginny's cauldron went flying; Mr. Weasley had thrown himself at Mr. Malfoy, knocking him backward into a bookshelf.' Arthur initiates full physical contact — he actually tackles Malfoy. He is then pulled apart by Hagrid and ends the scene with a cut lip.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1 (Flourish and Blotts): 'Mr. Weasley moves to hit Lucius Malfoy. Hagrid steps forward, puts a firm hand on Mr. Weasley's shoulder.' Arthur is stopped before landing a blow. He backs away. Hagrid's restraint precedes any contact.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, Arthur's tackle is a rare, unguarded eruption of genuine fury — a mild-mannered man pushed past his limit by a direct insult to his family's poverty and his Muggle-born associates. It costs him (cut lip, public embarrassment, Molly's fury) but it is authentically his action. In the film, Hagrid neutralises him before he acts, reducing Arthur from an agent of his own anger to someone who merely attempts something and is managed. This significantly softens his capacity for passionate, principled fury and weakens the moment that most clearly shows Malfoy has a real enemy in Arthur, not just an irritant.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Slytherin common room) – Arthur's fine reported without his response or inquiry at work
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 117–120: The newspaper clipping reports Arthur fined fifty Galleons and facing calls for his resignation. Book Scene 108 establishes that 'Mr. Weasley was facing an inquiry at work' and Harry burns with guilt over it. The professional and personal consequences for Arthur are registered as real ongoing damage to his career and family.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: Malfoy reads the newspaper aloud in the Slytherin common room ('Arthur Weasley… fined fifty Galleons… Muggle Protection Act should be scrapped immediately'). The scene functions to give Harry/Ron-as-Crabbe/Goyle information. There is no subsequent film scene showing Harry's guilt about Arthur's inquiry or any consequence for Arthur's career.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses Arthur's professional jeopardy to deepen Harry's guilt and to show that Arthur bears real costs for his values. The film uses the same newspaper beat purely as a plot-information device in the Polyjuice scene. The emotional consequence for Harry and the ongoing professional cost to Arthur are lost, reducing Arthur's sacrifice to background noise.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Dumbledore's office finale) – Arthur's 'flabbergasted' parenting speech transferred to Molly
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 139: In Dumbledore's office after Ginny's rescue, it is Arthur who delivers the parental lesson: 'Ginny! Haven't I taught you anything. What have I always told you? Never trust anything that can think for itself if you can't see where it keeps its brain? Why didn't you show the diary to me, or your mother?' Arthur is the one who identifies the exact failure, names his own prior teaching, and directly challenges Ginny.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4 (Dumbledore's office / corridor outside): The line is given to Mrs. Weasley, heard as she leads Ginny away: 'A diary that writes back to you! Honestly, Ginny! What were you thinking? Haven't I always told you? Never trust anything that can think for itself if you can't see where it keeps its brain!' Arthur is described as exiting 'still looking deeply shaken' in the book, but in the film he has no dialogue in this moment at all.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of Arthur's most substantive parenting moments in the entire book — he is not just warm or funny but actually wise and specifically prepared, having anticipated this class of danger and tried to teach his children about it. Transferring the speech to Molly erases Arthur's role as an active, knowledgeable parent and collapses his characterisation further into the 'bumbling enthusiast' register, while Molly (already the dominant disciplinarian) absorbs another of his meaningful functions.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Dumbledore's office finale) – Dumbledore's warning to Lucius about Arthur
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 150: Dumbledore explicitly warns Lucius: 'I would advise you, Lucius, not to go giving out any more of Lord Voldemort's old school things. If any more of them find their way into innocent hands, I think Arthur Weasley, for one, will make sure they are traced back to you.' Arthur is named by Dumbledore as a specific, credible threat to Lucius — someone with the institutional knowledge and motivation to pursue him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4 (Dumbledore's office): Dumbledore's warning is phrased as: 'One only hopes that no more of Lord Voldemort's old school things find their way into innocent hands. The consequences for the one responsible could be… severe.' Arthur is not named. The warning is general and impersonal.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version positions Arthur as an active institutional check on Lucius Malfoy — someone Dumbledore specifically identifies as capable and motivated to pursue accountability. The film's version removes Arthur from this equation entirely, reducing him from a named threat to an absent background figure. This matters for Arthur's function as a meaningful antagonist to the Malfoy agenda throughout the saga.

main_damage_causes: Consistent compression of Arthur's domestic and professional texture into comic-relief beats, stripping the exhaustion, legal cunning, and intellectual respect that distinguish him from a one-note Muggle enthusiast

Transfer of two of Arthur's most substantive agency moments — the physical confrontation with Malfoy and the parenting speech to Ginny — to other characters (Hagrid restrains him before contact; Molly delivers the diary warning), reducing him from an active agent to a managed or replaced one

Erasure of Arthur's role in Harry's surrogate-family relationship: the glasses repair, the dinner-table interrogation pattern, and the guilt Harry feels over Arthur's professional jeopardy are all absent, weakening the emotional foundation of the Weasley-as-Harry's-true-family theme
